questions.question: Chemical pathology
options: Is concerned solely with the analysis of blood samples and other body fluids in the laboratory
Involves the use of biochemical techniques to make diagnosis
The discipline is minimally affected by scientific advances
Provides the basis of structural defects in tissues otherwise known as pathophysiology
questions.explanation: Chemical pathology (clinical biochemistry) is the branch of laboratory medicine that uses biochemical analyses of blood, urine, CSF and other body fluids to make a diagnosis and to monitor and manage disease. It goes far beyond routine sample analysis and is continually reshaped by scientific and technological advances.

questions.question: The role of a consultant chemical pathologist is to
options: Provide detailed directions to other clinicians on patient management procedures
Provide advice to patients on drug-to-drug interactions (Therapeutic Drug Monitoring)
Interpret test results and suggest further line of management to other Clinicians
The analyses of body fluids sent to the laboratory by clinicians for the purpose of making a diagnosis
questions.explanation: The consultant chemical pathologist is the clinician overseeing the laboratory who guides other clinicians on the appropriate use and interpretation of investigations and on further management steps that follow from laboratory results. Routine analysis of fluids is the work of biomedical scientists, not the personal task of the consultant.

questions.question: In the Clinical Laboratory organogram
options: In Nigeria, the head of all clinical laboratory by law must be a pathologist the day-to-day activities of the
The technical head of the laboratory (MLS) oversees resident doctors in the clinical laboratory
The pathologist is particularly interested in the results outcomes
The reliability for the quality of results and reports generated by the clinical laboratory is the sole responsibility of the pathologist
questions.explanation: In the laboratory, although day-to-day technical work is delegated to Medical Laboratory Scientists (MLS), the pathologist leads the laboratory and bears ultimate accountability for the accuracy, quality and reliability of all results and reports generated. Quality and reliability of laboratory output therefore rest finally with the pathologist.

questions.question: In requesting for laboratory tests
options: The choice of the most appropriate test can impact minimally on the management of the patient
Urinalysis is a minimally invasive test
It is usually necessary-after a good history and clinical examination
Their value must be determined even before they are made
questions.explanation: Laboratory tests are requested as an extension of clinical assessment: they become necessary after a good history and clinical examination have raised diagnostic possibilities. Investigations then confirm, exclude or refine the clinical suspicion rather than replace the clinical examination.

questions.question: In dynamic function tests
options: A substance is usually monitored at time intervals
Gross changes are likely to be missed and will require the performance of more complicated tests
Random plasma glucose is a good example
Fasting plasma glucose is an excellent example
questions.explanation: Dynamic function tests (e.g., oral glucose tolerance test, ACTH stimulation, dexamethasone suppression, growth-hormone provocation) assess endocrine function by monitoring the change in a substance at timed intervals after a stimulus or a suppression. Static single measurements may miss the dynamic response, so serial timed sampling is the essence of these tests.

questions.question: Which of the following hormones play a pivot role in bone resorption?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is the principal hormone driving bone resorption: it acts on osteoblasts, which in turn stimulate osteoclasts to resorb bone, mobilising calcium and phosphate into the circulation. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (isoform 5b) is only an osteoclast marker of resorbing activity, not the hormonal driver. Bone alkaline phosphatase is a marker of bone formation (osteoblast activity).

questions.question: Which of the following is found in a 2-minute old baby?
questions.explanation: IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta (via FcRn-dependent active transport), so a newborn has predominantly maternal IgG in its circulation at birth. IgM, IgA1 and IgA2 do not cross the placenta and are synthesised by the infant only later.

questions.question: Which of the following cells is involved in innate immunity?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the professional antigen-presenting cells of the innate immune system: through pattern-recognition receptors (e.g., Toll-like receptors) they sense conserved microbial structures and initiate innate responses, then migrate to lymph nodes to activate adaptive T-cell immunity. Neutrophils and macrophages are also innate cells, but the cytotoxic T cell belongs to the adaptive immune system.

questions.question: One of these is not involve in decision making of patient management
questions.explanation: Algorithms, diagnostic criteria and reference intervals are all tools that directly guide clinical decisions about investigation and management. An organogram is merely the organisational chart showing the hierarchy of a laboratory or establishment; it plays no role in patient-management decisions.

questions.question: Which of these is not a tropic hormone
questions.explanation: Tropic hormones act on other endocrine glands to stimulate hormone secretion (e.g., ACTH on the adrenal cortex, LH/FSH on the gonads, prolactin on the breast). Cortisol is an effector hormone produced by the adrenal cortex in response to ACTH; it is not a tropic hormone.

questions.question: A common cause of hypocortisolism is
questions.explanation: Adrenal tuberculosis (with autoimmune adrenalitis, adrenal haemorrhage and metastases) destroys the adrenal cortex causing primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison's disease) with cortisol deficiency — hypocortisolism. Endogenous depression, alcohol abuse and severe obesity are associated with elevated (not reduced) cortisol.

questions.question: Biochemical features suggestive of Adrenal hyperfunction include
questions.explanation: Adrenal hyperfunction (e.g., Cushing's syndrome) produces cortisol excess with intrinsic mineralocorticoid (sodium-retaining) activity, causing sodium and water retention — therefore hypernatraemia (together with hypokalaemia and alkalosis). Hypoglycaemia and Addisonian crisis are features of adrenal hypofunction.

questions.question: Insulin dependent cells do not include
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes take up glucose through the insulin-independent GLUT2 transporter, so hepatic glucose uptake does not require insulin. Insulin-dependent glucose uptake occurs in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue via insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation, making muscle the classic 'insulin-dependent' tissue.

questions.question: In diabetic ketoacidosis;
questions.explanation: In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin deficiency allows potassium to move out of cells, and acidosis promotes H+/K+ exchange, so plasma potassium is characteristically raised (hyperkalaemia) even though total body potassium is usually depleted. DKA produces hyperosmolality, metabolic (keto)acidosis and high urine specific gravity.

questions.question: One of the following is not a marker for type 1 DM
questions.explanation: The recognised autoantibody markers of type 1 diabetes are islet-cell cytoplasmic antibodies (ICA), glutamic-acid-decarboxylase-65 (GAD65) antibodies, insulinoma-associated (IA-2) antibodies, insulin autoantibodies (IAA) and zinc-transporter-8 (ZnT8) antibodies. 'ZnT9' does not exist — the marker is ZnT8, so this is not a type 1 marker.

questions.question: Metabolic acidosis is primarily a problem of
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis results from a primary deficit of bicarbonate (base deficit) — either bicarbonate is lost (diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis) or it is consumed in buffering accumulated acid (ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure). Plasma bicarbonate therefore falls, with a decreased pH. It is primarily a problem of base (bicarbonate) deficit.

questions.question: Types of automation do not include
questions.explanation: The recognised categories of laboratory automation are total (full) laboratory automation, modular integrated systems and stand-alone (discrete) analysers. 'Mid-end automation' is not an established classification of laboratory automation.

questions.question: An effective physiologic buffer is
options: Buffer with pka closer to the pH of plasma
questions.explanation: A buffer is most effective when its pKa is close to the pH of the fluid it must buffer, because buffering capacity is maximal within about ±1 pH unit of the pKa. The bicarbonate system, whose effective pKa is near 7.4 in the open physiological system, is therefore the major extracellular physiological buffer.

questions.question: A goal of automation is to
questions.explanation: A principal goal of laboratory automation is to shorten turnaround time (the interval from sample receipt to result), along with improving throughput, precision, traceability and operator safety. Automation reduces TAT but can never eliminate it.

questions.question: One of the following is not an acute porphyria
questions.explanation: The acute porphyrias — acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria, variegate porphyria and ALAD-deficiency porphyria — present with acute neurovisceral attacks (abdominal pain, neuropathy, neuropsychiatric features). Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Günther's disease) is a chronic cutaneous porphyria with severe photosensitivity and haemolysis, not acute attacks.

questions.question: Clinical relevance of laboratory tests is not associated with
questions.explanation: Clinical relevance concerns the usefulness of a test in clinical decision-making — its precision, sensitivity, specificity and its role in diagnosis and patient follow-up. The individual analyst performing the test is an operational/personnel factor, not a determinant of a test's clinical relevance.

questions.question: Concerning glycated haemoglobin (HbA1C) the following is correct
options: Sample bottles for collecting blood sample is fluoride oxalate
Values of 5.9% are in the normal range
It is a ketoamine formed by non-enzymatic reaction of haemoglobin and fructose
HbA1C of 5% will give an estimated average plasma glucose value of 18.3mmol/l
questions.explanation: HbA1c is measured on whole blood collected in an anticoagulant such as EDTA or fluoride oxalate (fluoride also arrests in-vitro glycolysis). The other statements are incorrect: 5.9% is above the normal range (<5.7%); HbA1c is a ketoamine/aldimine formed by the non-enzymatic reaction of haemoglobin with glucose (not fructose); and an HbA1c of 5% corresponds to an estimated average glucose of about 5.4 mmol/L (not 18.3).

questions.question: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is seen in a congenital disorder such as
questions.explanation: Rotor syndrome (like Dubin–Johnson syndrome) is an inherited defect of hepatic excretion of conjugated bilirubin, producing conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia. Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler–Najjar syndrome (types I and II) and Lucey–Driscoll syndrome all cause unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia.

questions.question: Which of the following responds to thirst?
questions.explanation: Thirst and arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH) are the two primary effector responses to hyperosmolality and hypovolaemia: hypothalamic osmoreceptors stimulate AVP release (water retention by the kidney) and activate the thirst centre to stimulate drinking. Both act together to restore body water.

questions.question: Interpreting laboratory test results involves
options: The use of reference of intervals
Group based reference intervals are most reliable if available
The use of 90% of healthy individuals that fall outside the mean
The use of high-risk subjects as reference
questions.explanation: Where available, group-based (partitioned) reference intervals — by age, sex, etc. — are more reliable than one global interval, because many analytes (creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, haemoglobin, estradiol) differ significantly between groups. Reference intervals are conventionally derived as the central 95% of a healthy reference population, not from high-risk subjects.

questions.question: Causes of type 2 diabetes mellitus include all except
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is driven by insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency, strongly associated with a sedentary lifestyle, obesity and preceding impaired glucose tolerance. Insulin autoantibodies indicate autoimmune destruction of beta cells and are a feature of type 1 diabetes, not a cause of type 2.

questions.question: Which of this analyte is affected by eating food?
questions.explanation: Triglycerides are the classic analyte that rises after eating (chylomicrons and VLDL increase postprandially), so samples for triglycerides and a lipid profile require prior fasting (9–12 hours). Total cholesterol, alkaline phosphatase and (to a minor degree, iron) are relatively little affected by a single meal — triglycerides show the strongest postprandial change.

questions.question: One the following is an inducible enzyme
questions.explanation: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is an inducible microsomal hepatic enzyme: its activity increases several-fold following enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, rifampicin, barbiturates, carbamazepine) and alcohol, making it a sensitive marker of enzyme induction and of alcohol-related liver disease. The transaminases and nucleotide phosphatases listed are not classically inducible.

questions.question: The analytical phase of laboratory investigation involves
options: Transportation of samples to the laboratory
questions.explanation: The analytical phase is the actual measurement step — combining sample with reagents, incubating the reaction, and measuring the signal. Transportation, accessioning and sample processing (centrifugation, aliquoting) all belong to the pre-analytical phase.

questions.question: Functional enzymes
options: Are always present in the plasma
Are always absent in the plasma
Are found in small concentration in the plasma
Are found in large concentration in the cell
questions.explanation: Functional plasma enzymes (clotting factors, complement, plasminogen, lipases) circulate constantly in plasma to perform a physiological function there. By contrast, non-functional (cellular) enzymes such as ALT and AST are normally present in only tiny amounts in plasma and rise when cells are damaged or leak.

questions.question: Phenylketonuria is an inborn error of metabolism that results from
questions.explanation: Classical phenylketonuria results from deficiency (mutations) of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine and accumulates to high levels. The excess phenylalanine is then transaminated to phenylpyruvate (and further to phenyllactate and phenylacetate), but the primary defect is the accumulation of phenylalanine.

questions.question: Concerning Nutrition
options: Chromium deficiency leads to glucose intolerance
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is required for normal DNA synthesis; its deficiency produces megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia — megaloblastosis. The other pairings are wrong: vitamin C (not B vitamins) is central to collagen synthesis and bone healing, vitamin A (retinol) — not vitamin D — is needed for night vision, and vitamin D regulates calcium metabolism.

questions.question: Which of these analytes is affected by age?
questions.explanation: Estradiol concentration changes markedly with age: it rises at puberty, cycles in reproductive life and falls to very low levels after the menopause. Sodium and potassium intervals are tightly regulated and age-independent, whereas estradiol is the classic age-dependent endocrine analyte.

questions.question: Onchronosis is a feature of
questions.explanation: Ochronosis — dark blue-black pigmentation of cartilage, sclera, tendons and skin with darkening urine — is the hallmark of alkaptonuria, caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, so homogentisic acid accumulates and oxidises to a melanin-like pigment that deposits in connective tissue. Maple syrup urine disease is a branch-chain aminoacidopathy and tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency is a hyperphenylalaninaemia; neither causes ochronosis.

questions.question: In collection preanalytical phase
options: The patient should be identified by at least one item e.g., name and this must be an active process
Prolonged use of tourniquet can result in pseudo-hyperkalemia from lactic acidosis
The phlebotomist is required to call the name of the patient during the active identification process to which the patient identifies themselves by responding to their names
The use of needle with size 24G for venipuncture will significantly reduce hemolysis
questions.explanation: Prolonged application of the tourniquet (>1 minute) causes venous stasis, haemoconcentration and local tissue ischaemia; the resulting hypoxia/lactic acidosis promotes potassium efflux from muscle and red cells, causing a spurious rise in potassium (pseudohyperkalaemia), in addition to haemoconcentration of cells and proteins. Correct practice is to release the tourniquet promptly (within ~1 minute) once the vein is entered.

questions.question: Which of the following statements holds true?
options: Insulinomas are usually associated with low c-peptide levels
Fasting plasma glucose of 7mmol/L (126mg/dl) is diagnostic of gestational diabetes mellitus
Oral glucose tolerance test for pregnant women is usually done at 12-20 weeks of gestation
Neonatal hypoglycemia is a common finding in infants of diabetic mothers
questions.explanation: Infants of diabetic mothers are exposed to maternal hyperglycaemia, producing fetal hyperinsulinaemia; after delivery the high insulin persists while the maternal glucose supply stops, causing rebound neonatal hypoglycaemia (with macrosomia). The other statements are wrong: insulinomas give high (not low) C-peptide, GDM is diagnosed by OGTT at 24–28 weeks (fasting glucose recognises diabetes in general), and the OGTT in pregnancy is done at 24–28 weeks, not 12–20.

questions.question: In establishing a reference interval which of these is absolutely necessary?
questions.explanation: A reference interval is meaningless without a well-defined reference population — healthy reference individuals from whom reference values are sampled according to standard protocols (e.g., CLSI C28). Defining the reference population (and partitioning by age/sex) is the essential prerequisite for establishing any reference interval.

questions.question: Hypoglycemia in homogentisic acid deficiency is as a result of
questions.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in carbohydrate oxidation and for transketolase in the pentose-phosphate pathway; its deficiency impairs glucose utilisation and gluconeogenesis, predisposing to hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis. Sodium, potassium and phosphate disturbances do not by themselves cause hypoglycaemia.

questions.question: Investigations that are helpful in the management of diabetic patients include all except;
questions.explanation: Diabetic patients are monitored with fasting lipid profile (dyslipidaemia), glycated haemoglobin (long-term glycaemic control) and microalbuminuria (early diabetic nephropathy/albuminuria screening). A heparin assay is used to monitor unfractionated-heparin (anticoagulant) therapy and has no place in diabetic management.

questions.question: Which of the following is likely to cause hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics are a classic cause of hyponatraemia: they increase sodium and water loss and impair urinary dilution in the distal tubule. Failure to drink and diabetes insipidus cause hypernatraemia (water deficit), and Cushing's syndrome causes sodium retention with normal or high sodium.

questions.question: One of these represents post-collection analytical variables
options: Blood samples for bilirubin assay require transport in an ice slurry to avoid haemolysis
Centrifuge performance should be checked periodically to ascertain their speed, timer and temperature
Specimen should be stored at 2-8°C if analysis is delayed for about 1 month or longer
Choosing the appropriate sample bottle is critical to obtaining the right results
questions.explanation: After blood is collected, samples pass through in-laboratory processing; centrifugation is a key post-collection processing step, and the centrifuge's performance (speed, timer, temperature) must be verified periodically to ensure proper separation of serum/plasma. Transport in an ice slurry, refrigerated storage and choice of collection bottle represent collection/transport (pre-laboratory) variables.

questions.question: Chain of custody
options: Is important in tracing results outcome
Is the collection of evidence for medicolegal reasons
Is the ability to safeguard samples
questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented, uninterrupted sequence of custody of a specimen — who collected, handled, stored, transferred and signed for it. It is essential for forensic/medicolegal samples, where the legal integrity and verifiability of the specimen must be beyond doubt.

questions.question: Triglycerides
options: They are produced in the small intestines, liver and adipose tissue
They are neutral fats, however, can interact with water during transport
They are triesters of glycerol and amino acids
In human nutrition, TG constitute 70% of tissue storage fat and are the predominant form of glyceryl ester found in plasma
questions.explanation: Triglycerides are synthesised in three main sites: enterocytes of the small intestine (from dietary fatty acids), hepatocytes (hepatic lipogenesis) and adipose tissue (storage site). They are triesters of glycerol with three fatty acids (not amino acids), they are neutral hydrophobic fats, and they constitute about 90% (not 70%) of stored fat in humans.

questions.question: The following disorders do not contribute to hyponatraemia except:
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome contributes to hyponatraemia through sodium loss, dilutional effects of oedema, and — importantly — pseudohyponatraemia caused by hyperlipidaemia (lipids occupy plasma volume and lower the measured sodium). Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) causes sodium retention with hypertension and normal-to-high sodium, and 'confusion' is a symptom, not a disorder.

questions.question: Fatty acids
options: Non-essential fatty acids are endogenous fatty acids that are synthesized in the human body
Their length varies and are classified according to the number of hydrogen ions present
Those of importance in human nutrition and metabolism are of the medium and long chain class
The double bonds of both plants and animals' origin are usually 2 carbon atoms apart
questions.explanation: Non-essential fatty acids are so-called because the human body can synthesise them de novo (from acetyl-CoA, e.g., palmitate). Essential fatty acids (linoleic and α-linolenic acid) cannot be made and must come from the diet. Fatty acids are classified by chain length (number of carbon atoms, not hydrogen ions), and the most important human metabolic fatty acids are of the long-chain class.

questions.question: The following statement holds true
options: The commonest type of diabetes is type 2DM
C-peptide levels are usually low in type 1 DM
Type 2DM has relationship with HLA DR3 and HLA DR4
Type 1 DM has a strong genetic basis
questions.explanation: C-peptide is co-secreted with insulin in equimolar amounts and reflects endogenous beta-cell secretion; in type 1 diabetes the autoimmune destruction of beta cells results in characteristically low or undetectable C-peptide. Although type 2 is indeed the commonest type, the statement assessed here as correct is the C-peptide finding. The HLA DR3/DR4 associations and the weak-concordance figures concern type 1, and type 2 has the stronger genetic/familial basis.

questions.question: Sample collected in the following container will not cause pseudohyponatremia
questions.explanation: A lithium heparin bottle contains no sodium, so it does not contaminate the sample or spuriously alter the measured sodium. Sodium-based anticoagulant bottles (sodium heparin, sodium citrate, 'heparinised sodium') add sodium to the sample and interfere with accurate sodium measurement, and can contribute to spurious electrolyte results.

questions.question: Lesch Nyhan syndrome is
questions.explanation: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is caused by deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) in the purine salvage pathway and is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait, affecting boys with hyperuricaemia, gout, choreoathetosis, intellectual disability and compulsive self-mutilation.

questions.question: In hyperuricemia
options: The salvage pathway is not affected
questions.explanation: In the common forms of hyperuricaemia, urate rises from purine overproduction and/or reduced renal excretion while the enzymes of the salvage pathway remain intact. Defective xanthine oxidase would actually lower urate (it is the enzyme generating uric acid), and humans have no functional uricase, so low uricase activity is not a mechanism of hyperuricaemia in man.

questions.question: One of these causes hypocalcemia:
questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome — massive cell breakdown, especially after chemotherapy — releases intracellular contents causing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia (calcium binds/precipitates with the excess phosphate). The other listed conditions are not recognised direct causes of hypocalcaemia.

questions.question: Hyperglycemia of malignancy can be due to
questions.explanation: Ectopic (paraneoplastic) ACTH production by tumours causes Cushing's syndrome; the resulting cortisol excess promotes gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, producing hyperglycaemia. Tumours secreting IGF-2 and insulinomas both cause hypoglycaemia (from insulin-like activity), not hyperglycaemia.

questions.question: Phospholipids
options: They are lipids that have phosphorus as a backbone
They contain three long chain fatty acids of 14 to 24 carbon atoms long
Plasma concentration is high in kwashiorkor, marasmus and other forms of malnutrition
questions.explanation: Phospholipids are amphipathic: each molecule has a polar (hydrophilic) phosphate-containing head group and non-polar (hydrophobic) fatty-acid tails, which allows them to form lipid bilayers of cell membranes. They contain two (not three) fatty acids esterified to glycerol, and their plasma concentrations fall (not rise) in malnutrition.

questions.question: Monitoring of plasma glucose in diabetes will best be achieved using:
questions.explanation: Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) reflects the average plasma glucose over the preceding 2–3 months and is the best indicator of long-term glycaemic control in diabetes. A fasting glucose is only a snapshot, a lipid profile monitors associated dyslipidaemia, and microalbuminuria screens for nephropathy.

questions.question: In refeeding syndrome
options: Proton pump inhibitor is a cause
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when feeding is resumed after prolonged starvation: the insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, producing dangerous dyselectrolytaemia — hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia — with risk of cardiac arrhythmias. Refeeding is the trigger; starvation is the pre-existing state, not a complication.

questions.question: Which the following statement is false
options: PTHrP is responsible for humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy
Hyponatremia can result from ADH producing tumours
Hypokalemia is a feature of tumour lysis syndrome
Hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia are features of tumour lysis
questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome releases intracellular potassium from lysed cells, so hyperkalaemia — not hypokalaemia — is the characteristic feature (together with hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia). The other statements are true: PTHrP mediates humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, and ADH-producing tumours cause SIADH-type hyponatraemia.

questions.question: Cholesterol
options: Cholesterol esters do not contain polar groups making them hydrophobic
They are synthesised by all cells of the body
Insulin inhibits Beta-hydroxy-Beta-methyl CoA (HMG CoA) reductase activity
It is a very good source of fuel
questions.explanation: Esterification of cholesterol with a fatty acid removes the free polar hydroxyl (−OH) group, so cholesterol esters lose polarity and become hydrophobic — which is why they form the non-polar core of lipoproteins. Insulin actually activates (does not inhibit) HMG-CoA reductase, and cholesterol is not a fuel source.

questions.question: Plasma lipoprotein
options: Lipoprotein (a) is pro-plasminogen and promotes clot lysis
Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) accounts for most of the turbidity of postprandial plasma
Chylomicrons contain apoB100 as the major lipoprotein
VLDL contains apoB100 as the apoprotein
questions.explanation: Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle whose distinctive apoprotein, apo(a), is highly homologous to plasminogen — this homology is the structural basis of the Lp(a)–plasminogen interaction. (Scientifically, note that Lp(a) actually inhibits fibrinolysis and is pro-thrombotic, chylomicrons carry apoB-48, and the clearly correct statement would be that VLDL carries one molecule of apoB-100. This item's keyed answer is the apo(a)–plasminogen homology.)

questions.question: Apolipoproteins
options: Are protein portion of esterified cholesterol
Are the protein component of the lipoprotein
questions.explanation: Apolipoproteins are the protein components of lipoproteins. They provide structural stability to the particle and functional roles as ligands for cell-surface receptors (e.g., apoB-100 for the LDL receptor, apoE for hepatic receptors) and as cofactors for enzymes (apoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, apoA-I activates LCAT). They form only ~10–20% of lipoprotein mass; the bulk is lipid.

questions.question: Concerning oral glucose tolerance test
options: Loading dose of 95 mg of glucose is usually given to adult patients
In children, dose of glucose is given at 1.95g/kg body weight
Flat curve of OGTT can be caused by malabsorption syndrome
Hypoglycemic episodes are usually diagnosed by OGTT
questions.explanation: A flat (flatlined) glucose curve during an OGTT is characteristic of malabsorption — little glucose reaches the circulation from the gut, so glucose rises little. The adult standard is 75 g of glucose (1.75 g/kg in children, maximum 75 g), and spontaneous hypoglycaemia is not diagnosed by OGTT but by supervised fast/Whipple's triad.

questions.question: Lipid profile
options: LDL-C value can be derived from the Frederickson's formula
Total cholesterol concentration is largely unaffected by time of last meal
Fasting for at least 15 hours is a major requirement
questions.explanation: LDL-cholesterol is usually estimated (rather than directly measured) from the fasting lipid values using the Friedewald equation: LDL = total cholesterol − HDL − (triglycerides/2.2) in mmol/L (TG/5 in mg/dL), valid when triglycerides are below ~4.5 mmol/L. Fasting for 9–12 hours (not 15) is required for the profile; chylomicrons are absent from a proper fasting sample.

questions.question: One the following is non-essential amino acid:
questions.explanation: Glycine is a non-essential amino acid because the body can synthesise it (from serine and glyoxylate). Lysine, threonine and methionine are essential amino acids that must be supplied by the diet.

questions.question: Concerning cerebrospinal fluid
options: CSF protein is lowest at the lumbar region
In viral meningitis plasma glucose levels are very low
In bacterial meningitis, the CSF glucose is usually decreased
questions.explanation: In bacterial meningitis, bacteria and polymorphonuclear cells in the CSF consume glucose, so the CSF glucose is characteristically low (<50% of the simultaneous plasma glucose), with high protein, high neutrophils and a positive Gram stain/culture. In viral meningitis glucose is usually normal, CSF protein is lowest near the ventricles (highest in the lumbar sac, not lowest), and CSF volume is ~120–150 mL in adults.

questions.question: In obesity
options: Extra calories are produced majorly by fatty diet
questions.explanation: Obesity is strongly associated with insulin resistance (reduced insulin sensitivity) through excess adiposity, ectopic fat accumulation and altered adipokine signalling. Leptin levels are raised (not low) in obesity reflecting leptin resistance, and although BMR rises with fat-free mass, the key metabolic point assessed here is insulin resistance.

questions.question: In the elderly patient
options: Differentiating pathologic conditions and age-related changes is not difficult
Disease presentation may be atypical with nonspecific symptoms
Special consideration must not be emphasised during sample collection
Reference intervals are always the same as in middle age
questions.explanation: In elderly patients disease often presents atypically — silent myocardial infarction, confusion, falls, functional decline — rather than with classic textbook features. Because age-related physiological decline overlaps with pathology, differentiating them is genuinely difficult, special care is needed in sample collection (fragile veins), and reference intervals may differ from middle age.

questions.question: Biochemical changes due to ageing may be due to
questions.explanation: Ageing is associated with a decrease in muscle mass (sarcopenia) and a relative increase in body fat, with a fall in total body water (not an increase), alterations in renal/hepatic function and a rise (not a fall) in plasma lipids in many individuals.

questions.question: In paediatric patient
options: Reference interval changes with the age
Volume of blood is not a problem
There's increase fluid loss after 48 hours due to mature epidermis
Hypermagnesemia is usually seen in term babies because of overweight
questions.explanation: In children, reference intervals change with age from birth through infancy, childhood and puberty, because body composition, organ maturation and hormone concentrations all change (e.g., alkaline phosphatase peaks at growth spurts, creatinine rises with muscle mass). Blood volume is small so the volume drawn must be strictly controlled, and the newborn epidermis is immature, increasing (not decreasing) transepidermal fluid loss.

questions.question: In syndrome X
options: A diagnosis can be made only if 5 criteria are present
Waist circumference >88 cm in females is a criterion
Acanthosis nigrican is a major criterion
Inflammation is a possible risk factor
questions.explanation: Chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognised as a contributing mechanism in the metabolic syndrome ('syndrome X'): raised inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and CRP are linked to insulin resistance and its complications. Diagnosis (ATP III) requires at least 3 of 5 criteria, waist >88 cm in females is indeed a diagnostic criterion, and acanthosis nigricans is a sign of insulin resistance rather than a formal diagnostic criterion.

questions.question: Pre-analytical variables
options: Are factors that occur outside the laboratory for which the laboratory has no control
They account for less than 50% of total errors in the laboratory process
Modifiable factors will include circadian variation, gender and prolonged bed rest
Transcription errors cannot be minimised by computerization of laboratory requests
questions.explanation: Pre-analytical variables are the biological, collection, transport and handling factors that occur before analysis — many of them outside the laboratory's control — and they account for the majority (about 60–70%, i.e., over 50%) of total laboratory errors. Circadian variation, gender and posture/bed rest are biological (non-modifiable) factors, while the phlebotomy technique and tourniquet use are modifiable; computerisation reduces transcription errors.

questions.question: In chemical pathology laboratory
options: The use of quality control material is obligatory
Quality planning measures the modification of goals and objectives of the Laboratory
Quality improvement is aimed at eliminating the problem permanently
Quality control materials must be prepared in-house always
questions.explanation: Quality improvement is the systematic process of identifying the root cause of a problem and eliminating it permanently (rather than merely detecting errors after the fact). Quality planning sets goals, the use of QC material is also obligatory (and may be commercial or in-house), so the statement about permanently eliminating the problem describes quality improvement.

questions.question: Oral glucose tolerance test
options: It is used to diagnose relapse of diabetes mellitus
Is the gold standard for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus
It is a screening test for Diabetes mellitus
95g of glucose in 350 mL of water is the ideal
questions.explanation: The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is regarded as the gold-standard/reference test for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and of the intermediate states of glucose tolerance, because it directly evaluates glucose handling after a standard 75 g glucose load. Screening is done with fasting/random glucose or urinalysis; the adult load is 75 g, not 95 g.

questions.question: Factors that can trigger type 2 DM may include:
options: Persistent exposure to bovine milk protein during infancy
questions.explanation: Chronic overnutrition is the cardinal environmental trigger for type 2 diabetes: sustained caloric excess leads to obesity, ectopic fat and insulin resistance. Exclusive breastfeeding is regarded as protective, while persistent exposure to bovine milk protein and viral infections are immunologically implicated in the development of type 1 (not type 2) diabetes.

questions.question: In Type I DM
options: Steroid overdose is a risk factor
Insulin resistance is a major risk factor
Concordance rate for a set of identical twins is 90%
It is due to cell-mediated destruction of beta cells of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency with characteristic autoantibodies (ICA, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8). Steroid use and insulin resistance are type 2 mechanisms, and the identical-twin concordance is low for type 1 (~30–50%) but high (~90%) for type 2.

questions.question: Concerning point of care diagnosis
options: Reference intervals maybe different from conventional laboratory methods
Urgent samples cannot be assayed by point of care diagnostics
Point of care diagnostics require large volume of samples
Urinalysis strip is not a point of care service
questions.explanation: Point-of-care (POC/near-patient) devices use different sample types (often capillary whole blood) and methods from central laboratory analysers, so their reference intervals may differ from conventional laboratory methods. POC testing is rapid, uses small volumes and is ideal for urgent/bedside samples; urine dipstick testing is a classic point-of-care service.

questions.question: Concern in hypoglycemia
options: In adults it is defined by a value of 2.2mmol/L of plasma glucose
Dizziness is a sensorineural symptom associated with hypoglycemia
Thiazide diuretics have a side effect of hypoglycemia
Whipple's triad is used in the diagnosis of hypoglycemia
questions.explanation: Whipple's triad — (1) symptoms of hypoglycaemia, (2) documented low plasma glucose, and (3) relief of symptoms on glucose administration — is the classic criteria for diagnosing hypoglycaemia (especially in insulinoma evaluation). True hypoglycaemia in adults is conventionally diagnosed below 3.0 mmol/L, dizziness is a neuroglycopenic (not sensorineural) symptom, and thiazides cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.

questions.question: Occupations involving prolonged standing may cause
questions.explanation: Proteinuria that appears with prolonged standing/upright posture (renal venous congestion and haemodynamic changes) and disappears on recumbency is orthostatic (postural) proteinuria — a benign condition common in adolescents. Transient proteinuria follows exercise/fever; overflow proteinuria occurs when low-molecular-weight proteins exceed tubular reabsorption; apparent proteinuria is due to contaminating substances.

questions.question: In managing an unconscious patient, tests needed in the emergency room side line does not include
questions.explanation: In the emergency evaluation of an unconscious patient the priority bedside considerations are glucose estimation (hypoglycaemia), electrolytes/urea and acid-base status, and CSF chemistry when meningitis is suspected — these address the common metabolic and infective causes of coma. Urinalysis is not among the essential emergency side-line (near-patient) tests in the initial workup, making it the item that 'does not include'.

questions.question: Which of these conditions will cause hypocalcemia?
questions.explanation: Osteomalacia (and rickets), due to vitamin D deficiency, impairs intestinal calcium absorption, producing a low or low-normal serum calcium with characteristically low phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase. Vitamin A toxicity, immobilisation and osteolytic bone metastases all tend to raise (hypercalcaemia) rather than lower the calcium.

questions.question: Hypercalcemia can result from?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism — excess PTH from a parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia — is a leading cause of hypercalcaemia: PTH increases bone resorption, renal tubular calcium reabsorption and calcitriol production. Acute pancreatitis, high calcitonin and rickets are associated with hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia.

questions.question: All are examples of glycated proteins except
questions.explanation: Glycated proteins are formed by the non-enzymatic attachment of glucose to proteins: haemoglobin forms HbA1c, albumin forms fructosamine, and long-lived proteins accumulate advanced glycation end-products (AGEs). Sorbitol is a polyol produced inside cells from glucose by aldose reductase (polyol pathway); it is a sugar alcohol, not a glycated protein.

questions.question: Features of Von Gierke's disease do not include
questions.explanation: Von Gierke's disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is due to deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase and presents with severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis (metabolic acidosis) and hyperlipidaemia, with hepatomegaly and growth failure. Splenomegaly is not a feature — the liver (not the spleen) is the affected glycogen-storing organ.

questions.question: The following pairing is correct
questions.explanation: Whipple's triad (hypoglycaemia symptoms + low plasma glucose + relief with glucose) is the criteria used to diagnose hypoglycaemia. The other pairings are wrong: the well-fed (fed) state suppresses ketogenesis (starvation causes ketosis), lipoproteins are lipid–protein complexes (not carbohydrates), and Addison's disease causes hypoglycaemia — not hyperglycaemia.

questions.question: The following is wrongly matched
questions.explanation: The recognised associations are: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) with sodium retention/hypertension (± hypernatraemia), Cushing's syndrome with hypercortisolism, and acanthosis nigricans with hyperinsulinaemia/insulin resistance. Polycystic ovary syndrome is in fact ALSO strongly associated with hyperinsulinaemia/insulin resistance, so this keyed pair is scientifically questionable — the question intends it as the 'wrongly matched' pair, but it should be reviewed against the course material.

questions.question: The most correct sequence is represented by one of the following
options: Instruction, payment, sample collection, analysis, result transcription
Result transcription, instruction, analysis, sample collection
Instruction, payment, sample collection, transportation, analysis
Sample collection, payment, transportation, analysis, result transcription
questions.explanation: The correct sequence of the total laboratory testing process is: clinician's instruction (test request) → payment/transaction (accessioning of the request) → sample collection → analysis → transcription (validation) and delivery of the result to the requesting clinician. Options that omit payment after instruction or place result transcription first are wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following is true?
options: Liver Cirrhosis and hepatitis D virus
questions.explanation: Porphyrias are disorders of haem (haem) biosynthesis — inherited enzyme defects along the haem synthetic pathway cause accumulation of porphyrins and precursors. Sickle cell disease reflects a mutation in the β-globin (haemoglobin) chain, not 'globulin'; cirrhosis is associated with hepatitis B/C (HDV only infects alongside HBV); and haemolysis increases urobilinogen (acholic urine — pale, absent bile pigment — is a feature of obstructive jaundice).

questions.question: In severe diarrhoea
questions.explanation: Severe diarrhoea causes loss of intestinal secretions rich in sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate, so chloride is lost with hypochloraemia and a metabolic acidosis develops (bicarbonate is also lost, producing a base deficit). Alkalosis does not supervene — bicarbonate loss drives the pH down.

questions.question: Identify the correct sequence
questions.explanation: In the hospital/clinical-laboratory organisational hierarchy the chain of authority descends: Chief Medical Director (CMD) → Chairman of the Medical Advisory Committee (CMAC) → Head of Department (HOD) → Consultants → Registrars (residents) → Coordinator → other (technical/support) staff.

questions.question: Jaundice
options: Prehepatic when caused by biliary atresia
Steatorrhoea is indicative of bile salts absence
Posthepatic may have excess urobilinogen in urine
questions.explanation: Steatorrhoea indicates absence/insufficiency of bile salts: bile salts are required to emulsify and micellise dietary fat, so biliary obstruction or severe liver-bile failure causes fat malabsorption with steatorrhoea. The other associations are wrong: biliary atresia causes post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice, post-hepatic obstruction reduces (not increases) urinary urobilinogen, and severe haemolysis produces pre-hepatic jaundice with raised urobilinogen.

questions.question: Turnaround time
options: Time from sample collection to time of analysis of sample
Time taken to process patient's sample after collection
Time from collection of sample to time result is received by the user
Time of sample collection to time of result transcription
questions.explanation: Turnaround time (TAT) is the total interval from sample collection to the time the result is received by the requesting user (clinician or patient). It is a key laboratory quality indicator and is broader than analysis time or the time to transcription alone.

questions.question: In newborn period
options: Blood volume is higher than total body water
ICF compartment is greater than ECF
ECF compartment is greater than ICF
questions.explanation: In the newborn, total body water is about 75% of body weight and — unlike the adult — the extracellular (ECF) compartment is proportionally larger than the intracellular (ICF) compartment (ECF ≈ 40–45%, ICF ≈ 30–35% of body weight). The exam key records 'ICF > ECF' (option B); this conflicts with standard neonatal physiology and should be checked against the course material.

questions.question: Gestational diabetes
options: Is diabetes noticed in the 28th week of pregnancy
Is diabetes noticed in the first trimester
questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diabetes (carbohydrate intolerance of variable severity) that is first detected during pregnancy — typically diagnosed by OGTT at 24–28 weeks. It differs from pre-existing diabetes, and although most cases resolve after delivery, affected women carry an increased future risk of type 2 diabetes.
